name: Piecewise Linear Mapping and Integration
text:
# Piecewise Linear Mapping and Integration

Also called: Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping

## Overview
This family defines opacity $\alpha$ as a piecewise linear function of the scalar volume data value $d$, serving as the foundational opacity mapping strategy for [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md). It distinguishes itself from analytical forms (e.g., polynomials [S1, unofficial]) and SDF-based derivations by using explicit linear segments between control points, offering computational simplicity and intuitive user control over tissue classification.

## Shared principles
The family relies on the parent's discretized volume rendering integral [G]. For each sample $i$ along the ray $r(t)$, the scalar value $d_i$ is obtained via interpolation [S2, unofficial][S5, unofficial]. The transfer function $T(d_i)$ maps this scalar to a color vector $C_i$ and a scalar opacity $\alpha_i$ [S2, unofficial][S5, unofficial]. These values are then used in the front-to-back [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) equations provided in the parent article [G]. The mapping is defined by a set of control points $(d_n, \alpha_n)$ such that $d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_N$. For a sample value $d_i$ falling within the interval $[d_n, d_{n+1}]$, the opacity is computed via linear interpolation:
$$
\alpha_i = \alpha_n \frac{d_{n+1} - d_i}{d_{n+1} - d_n} + \alpha_{n+1} \frac{d_i - d_n}{d_{n+1} - d_n}
$$
Values outside the range $[d_1, d_N]$ typically map to zero opacity [G]. The opacity $\alpha_i$ is strictly bounded within $[0, 1]$ for standard compositing, though some implementations may output intermediate values that are clamped [G].

## Subtopics

### [Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping with Gradient Scaling](1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md)
[1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md](1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md) renders volume data by mapping voxel scalar values to opacity using piecewise linear functions defined by tissue types, then scaling the resulting opacity by the magnitude of the local gradient vector to suppress tissue interiors and enhance bounding surfaces. Unlike [Linear Opacity Interpolation](7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md), which maps values directly to opacity without geometric weighting, this technique ensures that thin structures appear as faint wisps rather than holes, and that surface boundaries are visually emphasized over homogeneous regions. It requires the Adjacency Criteria: tissue types must be ordered by scalar value, and each tissue type must touch at most two other tissue types (specifically $n-1$ and $n+1$). Violations require interactive [clipping](#1444-clipping.md).

### [Linear Opacity Interpolation](7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md)
[7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md](7016-linear-opacity-interpolation.md) maps scalar volume data values to opacity using linear interpolation between two threshold values. It serves as the foundational opacity mapping technique within the Piecewise Linear Mapping and Integration family, providing a simple, computationally inexpensive method to define opacity transitions. Unlike its sibling [Piecewise Linear Opacity Mapping with Gradient Scaling](1335-piecewise-linear-opacity-mapping-with-gradient-scaling.md), which incorporates gradient magnitude to modulate opacity, this method relies solely on the scalar data value.

### Piecewise Linear Transfer Function Integration
A rendering technique that integrates piecewise linear transfer functions using a 2D texture map to compute correct exponential per-pixel opacity [S1, unofficial]. It uses a 2D texture map parameterized by opacity and thickness [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of piecewise linear transfer functions is a standard approach in volume visualization, allowing users to define opacity based on tissue types (e.g., CT numbers) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial]. The integration of these functions using hardware-accelerated texture maps for exponential opacity calculation is described in the context of GPU-based volume rendering of unstructured grids [S1, unofficial].
